paragraph.text: M4. "Being vegan is hard if you travel a lot"

traveling takes more planning for vegans, and sometimes the options are few. But almost every place has something without animal products: rice, beans, bread, fruit, vegetables, nuts. Restaurant-finder apps, supermarkets and a snack in the bag solve most cases. The difficulty justifies, at most, a rare and genuine exception, not giving up veganism at home, where most meals are eaten.
M. Ex-vegans: why I gave up ·
"I travel a lot for work. Being vegan on the road, in airports, in small towns is impossible. I gave up."
People who travel a lot depend on what they find along the way.
In many places, vegan options are few or nonexistent.
No one is obliged to go hungry or to eat poorly.
So people who travel a lot aren't obliged to be vegan.

P1 and P3 are true. P2 is sometimes true, but it's usually exaggerated. And the conclusion goes too far: even if some meals on a trip were difficult, that wouldn't justify eating animals at home or in places where there are options.
: it extends the difficulty of a few situations to a whole life.
"On the road, there's only fried snacks and cheese rolls."
"On a work trip, you can't choose."
"In another country, how am I supposed to know what's in the food?"
"Vegans don't travel, they just stay home."
"Eating out, traveling and parties become impossible." (which is J13)
"Nobody's perfect; I do what I can." (which is E6)

When we travel, we can bring a snack in our backpack: fruit, nuts, a sandwich. And almost everywhere there's rice, beans, bread or fruit. With a little planning, you can travel without eating animals.

Traveling does take more planning. But almost every place has something vegan, even if it's simple: rice, beans, bread, fruit, salad. A snack in the bag, a restaurant app and a supermarket solve most cases. And if somewhere there really is no option, that justifies an exception there, not dropping veganism at home.
"In how many of your meals this week do you really have no option at all?"
The argument uses the hardest case to decide all the others:
Snacks in the bag, simple dishes, supermarkets
In a remote place, with no option at all
As little harm as possible, as an exception

text.bold: 1. The difficulty concerns some meals, not all of them.

paragraph.text: Even people who travel a lot eat a good share of their meals in places with options. The conclusion of giving everything up doesn't follow from a few difficult meals.

text.bold: 2. Almost every place has basic vegan food.

paragraph.text: Rice, beans, bread, pasta with tomato sauce, fruit, vegetables, nuts. It may not be a special meal, but it's food.
Bringing snacks, looking up restaurants in apps, choosing accommodation with a kitchen, asking for adapted dishes. That's what people with allergies, religious restrictions or celiac disease do.
Restaurants, fast-food chains and supermarkets offer more and more vegan products, including on highways and in airports.

text.bold: 5. A genuine exception is different from giving up.

paragraph.text: If, in a remote place, there's nothing without animal products, eating the minimum needed there is an exception. That doesn't license eating animals at home.
Inconvenience was a reason for quitting for 13% of former vegetarians and vegans
Survey carried out in 2014 in the United States
(d) The strongest counter-reply: it's exhausting to live always planning
The most serious version says: the problem isn't one meal, but the fatigue of always having to plan, search, ask and explain. For someone who travels every week, that weighs on them.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
After a few trips, a person knows what to bring, where to stop and what to order. The effort shrinks over time.

text.bold: Fatigue justifies simplifying, not giving up.

paragraph.text: Eating the simplest dish, always bringing the same snack, having a few trusted places.

text.bold: The cost to animals doesn't shrink with fatigue.

paragraph.text: The discomfort of planning is still much smaller than the harm avoided.

Even if traveling made veganism more work, the question would remain the same: is it just to make animals suffer and die to avoid the work of planning a meal? Most of the time, the answer is a snack in the bag.
J9 "It's hard; I don't have time"
Lack of time is the underlying reason
M3 "Being vegan limited me when eating at my relatives' homes"
The same difficulty, away from home
J13 "Eating out, traveling and parties become impossible"
The difficulty of travel is extended to social life
E6 "Nobody's perfect; I do what I can"
From the difficulty of a few meals, concludes everything is impossible
From the hard case to the rule
Uses the remote place to decide what to do at home
Weighs the work of planning, not the harm to the animal

text.bold: Plans the rest of the trip.

paragraph.text: The difficult meal is remembered, the easy ones are forgotten
The usual menu seems the only one possible
The principle being tested is: "if a rule is hard in some situations, it can be dropped in all of them".
Someone who travels could stop following their religion at home too
Someone who travels could always eat gluten
Someone who can't find a recycling bin on a trip could stop recycling at home

It's right that traveling takes more planning, that in some places the options really are few and that the fatigue of always planning weighs on people. It's also right that no one should go hungry because of a rule.

But the difficulty of a few meals doesn't justify giving up veganism in all of them. The good answer is to share travel strategies, and to remember that genuine exceptions are different from giving up.
